ref: Augustine, Tractates on the Gospel of John 46
basis: Christ as good shepherd versus hireling
note: Augustine's exposition of John 10 reads the good shepherd's care and self-giving as Christological, giving a major Christian interpretive frame for the owner, flock, and protective contrast in the source.

basis: lost largest sheep sought over the ninety-nine
note: This Christian apocryphal version makes the wandering sheep the largest and specially loved one; it is a distinctive reception of the owner who actively seeks and values a member of the flock.

basis: source ر ع ي B002; Syriac rʿyā, shepherd
note: The Peshitta's Syriac rʿyā for Jesus as the good shepherd is cognate with Arabic rāʿī in the source and uses the shared root for self-giving flock care.

basis: plowman and thresher work in hope of a share
note: Paul states the human-worker application of the ox text: laborers should expect a share of the yield. It reframes the source's livestock provision as a principle about those who serve a community.

basis: one who tends a flock shares its milk
note: Paul's pastoral labor analogy assumes that the flock's keeper receives its produce, linking the source's pasture as provision with the work of tending it.

basis: Paul rereads the unmuzzled ox command for apostolic support
note: Paul cites the Torah's feeding of a working ox and asks how its principle bears on apostolic workers; this is a deliberate interpretive reapplication of animal provision, not simply a duplicate pasture image.

basis: the world passes away while the doer of God's will remains
note: The verse gives a direct Christian formulation of the source's distinction between the passing worldly life reached through temporary provision and what endures.

basis: All flesh like grass
note: The commentary reads pasture’s decay as a path toward worldly transience; Peter applies Isaiah’s grass-withering image to all flesh and human glory, making mortality explicit.

basis: all flesh like grass; grass withers
note: Peter applies fading grass to human mortality, a direct Christian extension of the source's pasture-to-debris and worldly-transience turn.

basis: word remains forever
note: The verse's enduring word completes the preceding grass image with a lasting contrast, comparable to the source's contrast between worldly life and what remains.

basis: Shepherd and guardian of souls
note: The commentary describes the shepherd as one who watches over and protects a flock; Peter says the addressees returned from straying like sheep to the shepherd and guardian of their souls, applying the image to spiritual oversight.

basis: return to shepherd and overseer of souls
note: Straying sheep return to a shepherd who is also an overseer, joining restoration, guidance, and supervisory care in the source's pastoral image.

basis: Leaders shepherd God’s flock
note: The commentary explicitly says a governor tends his subjects as a shepherd tends livestock; elders are told to shepherd God’s flock and oversee it willingly, applying the pastoral relation to community leadership.

basis: elders shepherd God's flock with oversight
note: The elders' charge makes shepherding a form of responsible oversight, giving a Christian communal application to the source's ruler who tends a people.

basis: Shepherding without domination
note: The commentary compares a ruler’s care for subjects with a shepherd’s care for livestock; Peter tells elders not to dominate those entrusted to them but to be examples, adding an ethical limit to pastoral authority.

basis: leaders do not dominate but become examples to the flock
note: The elders are forbidden to lord it over those entrusted to them and instead model conduct; it qualifies the source's ruler-shepherd relation with a specific non-dominating form of leadership.

basis: The chief shepherd
note: The commentary’s human ruler is a shepherd under the owner’s care; Peter calls Christ the chief Shepherd whose appearing brings a crown, making human oversight subordinate to divine shepherding.

basis: chief shepherd appears
note: The title chief shepherd places local shepherd-leaders under a higher shepherd, akin to the source's distinction between the owner and those who lead within the herd scene.

basis: seen things are temporary and unseen things eternal
note: Paul's temporal-eternal contrast is a close Christian formulation of the source's conclusion about the worldly life and the more enduring reality, though it does not itself use pasture imagery.

basis: Overseers shepherd God’s church
note: The commentary says a governor shepherds his subjects; Paul charges overseers to shepherd God’s church, which God acquired, making pastoral leadership both delegated and accountable.

basis: overseers shepherd God's acquired flock
note: The elders must watch over the whole flock and shepherd God's assembly; it makes pastoral rule explicitly attentive and accountable, resonating with B002 and the source's B003 watchfulness.

basis: fierce wolves will not spare the flock
note: Paul's warning supplies the threat that makes pastoral watchfulness necessary, sharpening the source's protective shepherd rather than repeating its generic title.

basis: pastors joined with teachers in communal leadership
note: The risen Christ gives pastors-and-teachers to the community, a concise Christian institutional use of shepherd language for guiding and forming people.

basis: The great shepherd of the sheep
note: The commentary’s Rab is owner and shepherd of the flock; Hebrews calls Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep, grounding pastoral leadership in God’s covenant and the raising of Jesus from the dead.

basis: Jesus the great shepherd of the sheep
note: The title great shepherd binds communal pastoral imagery to the God of peace and resurrection, a Christian theological development of the source's divine owner/shepherd.

basis: The good shepherd protects the sheep
note: The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who surrounds and preserves the animals; Jesus says the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, making protection costly and deliberate.

basis: good shepherd lays down life for sheep
note: The good shepherd's self-giving makes protection of the flock more radical than the source's lexical description of the shepherd who surrounds and preserves livestock.

basis: A failed guardian abandons the flock
note: The commentary’s shepherd protects livestock; the hired hand sees the wolf, abandons the sheep, and flees, dramatizing the difference between a true guardian and mere employment.

basis: hired hand does not own sheep and abandons them
note: The contrast hinges on ownership and guarding: a hireling flees while the true shepherd's sheep are endangered, a negative foil to the source's owner who protects the herd.

basis: Shepherd knows his own
note: The commentary describes a single owner’s care of a flock; Jesus knows his own sheep and is known by them, adding reciprocal recognition to ownership and tending.

basis: shepherd knows his own sheep
note: Mutual recognition between shepherd and sheep develops the source's closing move in which the person names this owner as his own Rab.

basis: eternal life and no snatching from the shepherd's hand
note: Jesus gives the sheep unending life and guarantees that no one will snatch them away, bringing the source's guarded flock and its lasting-life contrast together.

basis: The shepherd calls his own sheep
note: The commentary calls Rab the herd’s owner and describes the one who guides it; the shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining ownership to personal guidance.

basis: calls own sheep and leads them out
note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, an unusually exact New Testament counterpart to the source's owner and B003 animal-leader scene.

basis: Leading ahead of the flock
note: The commentary’s leaders among wild animals go ahead and guide the rest; Jesus’ shepherd goes ahead of his sheep and they follow, a close image of leading from the front.

basis: goes before sheep and they follow
note: The shepherd goes ahead of the sheep and they follow his known voice, directly realizing the commentary's detail of front animals guiding those behind.

basis: Sheep find pasture
note: The commentary’s owner guides the herd to pasture; Jesus says those entering through him will go in and out and find pasture, placing access to grazing within the shepherd image.

basis: go in and out and find pasture
note: Within the shepherd discourse, entering through Jesus leads to safety and pasture; it joins protection with access to grazing as in the source's unified scene.

basis: Peter told to shepherd Jesus’ sheep
note: The commentary extends the shepherd’s care to a ruler’s subjects; the risen Jesus tells Peter to shepherd his sheep, transferring pastoral responsibility to a human leader.

basis: commission to shepherd my sheep
note: The risen Jesus entrusts his own sheep to Peter's care, distinguishing the flock's owner from the human leader who is commissioned to tend it.

basis: Feed Jesus’ sheep
note: The commentary’s shepherd protects and tends livestock; Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep, specifying practical provision as part of the leadership charge.

basis: little flock and the Father's gift of the kingdom
note: Jesus calls the disciples a little flock while locating their security in the Father's gift of the kingdom, joining pastoral belonging with the source's movement beyond temporary worldly provision.

basis: Seeking the lost sheep
note: The commentary says the shepherd guards the flock and watches where matters lead; a shepherd searches for one lost sheep until he finds it, showing care as sustained attention to an outcome.

basis: owner seeks the one lost sheep
note: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost sheep, making the source's enclosing and preserving shepherd an active seeker rather than only a keeper of pasture.

basis: struck shepherd and scattered sheep
note: The passion prediction reverses the source's secure owner-and-flock scene: when the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter, showing the flock's dependence on its guide.

basis: Shepherd-less people and teaching
note: The commentary connects a shepherd’s guidance with care for a community; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins to teach them, showing guidance as an answer to that lack.

basis: crowd as sheep without shepherd; Jesus teaches
note: Jesus responds to a shepherdless crowd by teaching it, making guidance of people the action expected from the missing shepherd.

basis: ruler who will shepherd Israel
note: Matthew's citation calls the coming figure both ruler and shepherd of Israel, precisely echoing the source's ruler/shepherd equation.

basis: shepherd separates sheep from goats at judgment
note: The final judgment is pictured through a shepherd sorting a mixed herd; it gives the source's animal scene an eschatological use distinct from provisioning and protection.

basis: Grass here, then fuel
note: The commentary moves from pasture made waste to the temporary life of this world; Jesus contrasts grass in the field today with its being thrown into the oven tomorrow, using the plant’s short course to teach about trust in God’s provision.

basis: grass today, cast into an oven tomorrow
note: Jesus uses grass's brief life to teach trust in God's provision; the image closely meets the source's created pasture that soon changes, while its argument concerns anxious humans rather than livestock.

basis: People as sheep without a shepherd
note: The commentary extends shepherding from livestock to a ruler’s subjects; Jesus sees the crowds harassed and helpless like sheep without a shepherd, making the image a diagnosis of neglected people.

basis: A shepherd-king rules the nations
note: The commentary says a ruler shepherds his subjects; Revelation depicts the child destined to shepherd all nations with an iron rod, preserving the political shepherd image while giving it a forceful judgment register.

basis: ruling nations expressed by the shepherd verb
note: The royal judge's rule over nations is stated with the verb to shepherd, preserving the political sense of tending subjects foregrounded in source B002.

basis: flock no longer hungers or thirsts
note: The eschatological community's freedom from hunger and thirst supplies the provision that the following shepherd-and-springs image brings to completion, echoing the source's pasture and lasting-life movement.

basis: The Lamb shepherds and guides
note: The commentary’s scene brings a flock to pasture under its owner’s guidance; the Lamb shepherds the redeemed and guides them to springs of living water, joining shepherding with final provision.

basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs of life
note: The Lamb becomes the shepherd who guides the flock to living-water springs; it carries the source's pasture-and-guidance image into its own enduring, eschatological setting.

basis: angel of repentance appears as shepherd
note: Hermas receives moral commands from a shepherd figure; this later Christian use turns pastoral guidance into corrective formation, a plausible extension of the source's Rab-as-corrector within its herd image.

basis: Lord of sheep and accountable appointed shepherds
note: The Animal Apocalypse represents Israel as sheep under the Lord of the sheep and appointed shepherds whose stewardship is judged; it expands the source's owner, flock, and delegated leaders into an apocalyptic history.

basis: Moses’ compassion for a stray lamb
note: The commentary says a shepherd surrounds and protects animals and compares this to a ruler’s care of subjects; this midrash says Moses was chosen after he carried a tired lamb to water, interpreting leadership as attentive care for the vulnerable.

basis: Moses carries the thirsty straying lamb
note: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate attention to a runaway lamb the reason God entrusts Israel to him; it turns the source's Musa-and-shepherd scene into a criterion for protective leadership.

basis: Davidic king shepherds the Lord's flock faithfully
note: The psalm portrays the hoped-for Davidic ruler as faithfully shepherding the Lord's flock, preventing their stumbling in pasture and leading them in holiness; it fuses delegated rule, divine ownership, and guidance.

basis: leader must go out and come in before Israel
note: The exposition of Numbers 27:17 reads Moses's request as one for a leader present with the people rather than distant from them, sharpening the source's image of the animal that leads the others from in front.

basis: source ر ع ي B002; Aramaic rʿyā for shepherd
note: The Aramaic witness retains the congregation-as-sheep-without-a-shepherd image in Moses's succession request; its rʿyā is a cognate of the source's rāʿī and still carries public leadership.

basis: A shepherd protects his flock from predators
note: The commentary defines the shepherd as protecting livestock; David recounts pursuing a lion or bear that took a lamb from the flock, giving a concrete human example of pastoral guardianship.

basis: Rescuing the lamb from the predator
note: The commentary’s shepherd preserves the herd; David says he struck the predator and rescued the lamb from its mouth, specifying protection as active recovery.

basis: David pursues a predator and rescues the lamb
note: David's shepherding includes going after the lion or bear and delivering the sheep from its mouth, a concrete protective action for the source's keeper who guards livestock.

basis: just rule in the fear of God
note: David's oracle defines the God-fearing ruler whose effect is developed in the next verse; it supplies the governing member of the source's shepherd-ruler image.

basis: rain causes grass to sprout from the earth
note: The next line compares the just ruler's advent to light and rain that sprouts grass, a striking joining of righteous rule with the growth of the source's pasture.

basis: Shepherd and ruler are one role
note: The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Israel’s elders tell David that he will shepherd Israel and be its leader, explicitly joining pastoral care and political rule.

basis: ruler commissioned to shepherd Israel
note: Israel tells David that he will shepherd God's people and be their ruler; its royal formula is a precise analogue to the source's B002 equation of governor and shepherd.

basis: David taken from pasture and following sheep to rule Israel
note: God recalls taking David from following sheep to be prince over Israel, making the shepherd-to-ruler transition explicit rather than merely metaphorical.

basis: shepherd rescues remnants from a lion's mouth
note: Amos's image of a shepherd recovering only a leg or ear from a predator gives a grim, concrete limit case for the source's protecting shepherd.

basis: Grass in the fields for cattle
note: The commentary says God brings forth pasture and animals graze it; the promise of rain includes grass in the fields for cattle, making pasture provision part of the land’s gift.

basis: grass for livestock and food for people
note: The land blessing explicitly moves from grass supplied for cattle to human eating, paralleling the commentary's pasture as provision for both people and their animals.

basis: working ox must not be muzzled
note: The law protects an animal's access to food while it works, a concrete ethical analogue to the source's working camels and livestock sustained by grazing.

basis: Watching stars and refusing their worship
note: The commentary mentions star-watching as a secondary r-ʿ-y sense while assigning the ultimate oversight to the Lord; Deuteronomy warns Israel not to be drawn into bowing to the sun, moon, and stars, adding a caution about confusing observation with divine rule.

basis: wise instruction given by one shepherd
note: Ecclesiastes attributes wisdom that prods and steadies its hearers to one shepherd, extending the source's pastoral guide into correction and instruction.

basis: Moses protects shepherds and waters their flock
note: Moses drives away attackers and waters the flock for Midianite shepherds, a specific earlier portrayal of the protective action the source assigns to a shepherd.

basis: Moses as a shepherd before his mission
note: The commentary points to Moses’ answer to Pharaoh as its explicit grazing scene; Exodus first shows Moses shepherding Jethro’s flock and bringing it to Horeb, giving that speaker a prior pastoral setting without retelling the Pharaoh encounter.

basis: Moses pastures Jethro's flock to Horeb
note: The biblical Moses first appears at Horeb while tending and leading a flock; alongside the commentary's explicit Musa setting, this gives a concrete narrative pastoral setting without claiming the two accounts are the same scene.

basis: Owner seeks his flock
note: The commentary fuses owner and shepherd in one scene; God says he himself will search for and seek his sheep, making divine ownership active rather than merely possessive.

basis: Sheep gathered from danger
note: The commentary’s shepherd guards the flock; God rescues his sheep from the cloudy, dark day on which they were scattered, adding rescue at the moment of peril.

basis: Led out to pasture
note: The commentary’s owner guides a herd to pasture; God brings the sheep out from the peoples and feeds them on Israel’s mountains, joining gathering, guidance, and grazing.

basis: God gathers sheep and feeds them on mountains
note: God himself brings the scattered flock out, gathers it, and feeds it on the mountains; this is a particularly close scene of owner, leading, and pasture.

basis: Good pasture
note: The commentary calls the pasture protected and supplied; God feeds his sheep in good grazing land and on rich pasture, giving a direct counterpart to the image of pasture provided by its owner.

basis: good pasture and secure grazing land
note: The promised sheep receive good pasture and lie down in rich grazing land, supplying the protected-pasture element of the source without reducing it to a word match.

basis: source ر ع ي B002/B003/B007; Hebrew רעה and מרעה
note: The Hebrew verb for tending and noun for pasture are cognate with the source's ر ع ي family; here they describe God feeding sheep in a good pasture, including both the source's shepherd and marʿā senses.

basis: God shepherds and gives rest
note: The commentary’s Lord is the flock’s owner and the shepherd who guards it; God says he will shepherd his sheep and make them lie down, uniting those roles in the same figure.

basis: God himself pastures and gives rest
note: The divine speaker personally shepherds the flock and makes it lie down, the clearest biblical formulation of the commentary's owner who both leads and supplies the grazing place.

basis: Seeking and tending
note: The commentary’s shepherd protects the herd and watches where affairs will end; God seeks the lost, brings back the strayed, binds the injured, and strengthens the weak, while judging the fat and strong sheep.

basis: God seeks lost, restores strayed, binds injured, and strengthens weak
note: God's own response reverses failed leadership through specific acts of search, restoration, and healing, deepening the source's owner-protector scene.

basis: Sheep trample the pasture
note: The commentary pairs a protected pasture with a shepherd who guards it; Ezekiel asks why well-fed sheep trample the rest of the pasture, making care for shared grazing land part of the pastoral duty.

basis: Other sheep eat trampled pasture
note: The commentary’s pasture is a provision belonging to the flock; Ezekiel says God’s sheep must eat what the strong sheep have trampled, adding harm within the flock to the image.

basis: Shepherds and rulers
note: The commentary says the ruler tends his subjects like a shepherd tends livestock; Ezekiel indicts Israel’s shepherds for feeding themselves rather than the flock, making rule answerable to those cared for.

basis: shepherd-rulers feed themselves instead of flock
note: Ezekiel's indictment turns the source's ruler-as-shepherd image into a negative test: leaders who consume provision themselves fail the flock entrusted to them.

basis: One shepherd over the flock
note: The commentary makes the owner, the flock, and its guide parts of one scene; God promises one shepherd, his servant David, over the sheep, linking divine ownership with a human ruler’s care.

basis: David appointed as one shepherd
note: God appoints David as the flock's shepherd, preserving the distinction between the ultimate owner and a commissioned human ruler developed in the source.

basis: human sheep of God's pasture
note: The chapter's conclusion explicitly calls the people God's sheep and flock of his pasture, completing the source's owner, people, and grazing-place relation.

basis: Protecting the vulnerable
note: The commentary defines the shepherd as one who surrounds and protects livestock; Ezekiel’s bad shepherds do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or seek the lost, specifying failures of that care.

basis: failed shepherds do not strengthen, heal, bind, seek, or restore
note: The detailed catalogue says what pastoral rule owes the vulnerable flock; it concretizes the source's claim that the shepherd surrounds and preserves those in his care.

basis: Scattered sheep with no searcher
note: The commentary’s shepherd protects and watches over the herd; Ezekiel’s sheep wander across mountains and hills with no one searching for them, portraying the result when pastoral oversight fails.

basis: Green plants given to animals
note: The commentary presents the Lord as the one who brings forth pasture for herds; creation assigns every beast the green plant for food, placing animal grazing within God’s original provision.

basis: green vegetation assigned as animal food
note: The creation decree gives green plants to land animals for food, a direct scriptural counterpart to God bringing forth pasture for livestock.

basis: Stars as a sign of future outcome
note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch connects watching stars with seeing where an affair will end; God brings Abram outside to look at the stars as a sign of his future descendants, a related but distinct use of the heavens to frame what is to come.

basis: camels receive straw and fodder at a household
note: The servant's camels are unloaded and supplied with straw and fodder at the house, a specific narrative counterpart to the source's camels grazing around people and dwellings.

basis: source ر ع ي B002/B007; Hebrew רְעוּ pasture the flock
note: Jacob's well scene tells the herdsmen to water the flock and then go pasture it; the Hebrew cognate shows the source's ر ع ي family in an ordinary husbandry setting.

basis: Arabic رعى and Hebrew רעה
note: The commentary records Arabic رَعَى (source lexeme in its r-ʿ-y branches) for grazing and tending; Jacob uses Hebrew רעה while offering to pasture Laban’s flock, giving the pastoral sense a specific Semitic lexical counterpart.

basis: shepherd bears loss for animals torn or stolen
note: Jacob describes accepting liability for flock losses rather than passing them to the owner; this gives a demanding economic form to the source's protective shepherd.

basis: God as lifelong shepherd
note: The commentary develops Rab as owner and the flock’s protector; Jacob blesses his descendants through the God who shepherded him all his life, making the personal shepherd relation explicit.

basis: God has shepherded Jacob all his life
note: Jacob calls God the one who has been his shepherd throughout life, giving the source's personal naming of one's Rab a concentrated ancestral precedent.

basis: Shepherd of Israel
note: The commentary’s owner and guardian of the herd meets Jacob’s naming of Israel’s God as Shepherd and Rock; the image adds steadfast protection amid Joseph’s affliction.

basis: grazing leads to fullness, pride, and forgetting the owner
note: Hosea depicts pasture and fullness producing self-exaltation and forgetfulness of God, an ethical counterpoint to the source's pasture as temporary provision under its owner.

basis: ox knows owner; donkey its master's manger
note: Isaiah makes an animal's recognition of its owner and feeding-place a rebuke to Israel; it adds a reversal to the source's animal scene and its later naming of one's own Rab.

basis: a child leads reconciled wild and domestic animals
note: The future peace scene gives a child the action of leading a mixed animal company, an indirect but specific counterpart to the source's B003 image of a leader before other animals.

basis: cow and bear graze; lion eats straw like ox
note: The transformed creation is pictured through shared grazing and fodder among animals, a distinct eschatological extension of the source's pasture and livestock scene.

basis: Rain and forage for livestock
note: The commentary connects pasture brought forth by God with grazing animals; Isaiah promises rain for seed and fodder for livestock, then says the land’s produce will be rich, joining animal provision to the land’s yield.

basis: rain, abundant bread, and livestock grazing broad pasture
note: The promised divine rain produces abundance and broad pasture for cattle, directly matching the commentary's creator who produces grazing provision for people and animals.

basis: working oxen and donkeys eat prepared fodder
note: Farm animals receive rich fodder while doing agricultural work, a close counterpart to the source's B007 detail of working animals grazing around a settled community.

basis: Shepherd gathers and carries
note: The commentary’s shepherd surrounds and protects the animals; God gathers lambs in his arms and carries them close, making tender protection part of divine rule.

basis: gather, carry, and gently lead the flock
note: The divine shepherd gathers vulnerable lambs, carries them, and gently leads nursing ewes; it gives concrete protective actions to the source's guarded pasture and leading owner.

basis: Stars counted and called by God
note: The commentary’s r-ʿ-y branch includes watching the stars and connects oversight with knowing an outcome; Isaiah asks the reader to look at the created host, which God brings out by number and calls by name, relocating cosmic knowledge in the Creator.

basis: Flesh as grass
note: The commentary links pasture turning to debris with the transient worldly life; Isaiah compares all flesh to grass, making human fragility the point of the plant image.

basis: Grass withers
note: The commentary notes the pasture’s change into waste; Isaiah says grass withers when the breath of YHWH blows on it, adding divine sovereignty over its disappearance.

basis: grass withers when the LORD's breath blows
note: The grass fades under God's breath, furnishing a close biblical image for the source's pasture that is later made into dark debris and for its turn toward the temporary world.

basis: The enduring word contrasts with grass
note: The commentary’s pasture decays while its owner knows its end; Isaiah contrasts withering grass with the word of God that stands forever, making permanence the counterpoint to decay.

basis: grass fades but God's word endures
note: The contrast between fading grass and what endures gives a scriptural counterpart to the commentary's move from temporary worldly provision to the better, lasting life.

basis: A ruler called God’s shepherd
note: The commentary extends shepherding to rulers over people; Isaiah calls Cyrus God’s shepherd, who will carry out the rebuilding of Jerusalem, giving the political metaphor a foreign royal instance.

basis: God declares the end from the beginning
note: The source explicitly makes the pasture's maker one who sees what it will become; Isaiah's divine knowledge of end from beginning is a precise theological bridge for that secondary claim.

basis: guide to springs after hunger and thirst
note: The compassionate leader guides the redeemed to water after removing hunger and thirst, pairing direction with provision as the commentary does.

basis: pasture on every bare height
note: In the restoration promise, the released people feed along the ways and find pasture even on bare heights; it extends the source's pasture image into guided return and unexpected provision.

basis: Moses leads God’s flock through the sea
note: The commentary invokes Moses speaking of grazing to Pharaoh; Isaiah recalls the one who brought Moses and God’s flock up from the sea, connecting the named speaker with God’s shepherding in the Exodus deliverance.

basis: Failed shepherds scatter the flock
note: The commentary says a ruler shepherds and guards his people; Jeremiah condemns shepherds who destroy and scatter God’s pasture-sheep, showing that political care can fail the pastoral duty.

basis: Rulers answer for the flock
note: The commentary extends animal care to a ruler’s care of subjects; Jeremiah holds Israel’s shepherds responsible for not attending the flock, sharpening the ethical burden of that analogy.

basis: God gathers the scattered flock
note: The commentary’s owner shepherds a flock to its pasture; God promises to gather the remnant from the lands where he scattered them and bring them back, connecting divine ownership with restoration.

basis: Shepherds remove fear
note: The commentary glosses the shepherd as one who protects the herd; the promised shepherds will tend the people so they need not fear or be dismayed, spelling out the result of care.

basis: Shepherds feed with knowledge
note: The commentary says rulers shepherd their subjects and the herd’s leaders guide others; God promises shepherds who will feed the people with knowledge and understanding, specifying instruction as a form of guidance.

basis: shepherds after God's heart feed knowledge and understanding
note: God promises leaders who feed the people with knowledge and discernment, making pastoral governance an intellectual and moral guidance like the source's leading function.

basis: God gathers and keeps Israel as a shepherd
note: The one who scattered Israel gathers and guards it as a shepherd guards a flock, making protection and restoration integral to divine ownership.

basis: Bad shepherds lead sheep astray
note: The commentary’s herd leaders are those who guide others; Jeremiah describes lost sheep whose shepherds led them astray in the mountains, showing the same leadership relation reversed into misguidance.

basis: shepherds lead sheep astray from their resting place
note: The lost sheep are misdirected by their shepherds through the mountains and forget their resting place; this is a pointed negative reversal of the source's guide who brings a flock to pasture.

basis: God makes grass sprout in desolate ground
note: God satisfies wasteland and makes grass grow where people do not cultivate it; this extends the source's pasture-maker to nonhuman and wild terrain.

basis: Herds suffer when pasture fails
note: The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; Joel depicts cattle groaning and herds wandering because there is no pasture, showing the consequence for dependent animals when grazing land is lost.

basis: land belongs to God; people are temporary residents
note: God's ownership of land and the people's temporary tenancy give a land-based counterpart to the source's Rab-as-owner and its explanation of pasture as temporary metāʿ.

basis: ruler stands and shepherds in the LORD's strength
note: Micah joins rule, secure dwelling, and shepherding in the strength of God, a direct royal form of the source's ruler who tends his people.

basis: The ruler shepherds securely
note: The commentary says the ruler shepherds his subjects; Micah’s ruler stands and shepherds his flock in YHWH’s strength, after which the people dwell securely, joining leadership, divine backing, and protection.

basis: Moses gives water to congregation and livestock
note: God instructs Moses to bring water from the rock for both the people and their animals; it is a specific Mosaic scene of shared human-and-livestock provision.

basis: Leader before the flock
note: The commentary’s wild leaders guiding those behind them meets Moses’ request for a leader who goes out and comes in before Israel, lest the congregation be sheep without a shepherd; it connects guidance with accountable rule.

basis: leader goes before the people; sheep without shepherd
note: Moses asks for a successor who goes out before and brings in the congregation so it is not sheep without a shepherd; it directly joins the source's Musa setting, B003 leading-from-the-front, and ruler-as-shepherd.

basis: the righteous knows an animal's needs
note: The proverb makes attentive care for an animal a mark of righteousness, giving an ethical consequence to the source's shepherd who protects livestock.

basis: Know the state of the flock
note: The commentary describes a shepherd who watches where matters will lead and a ruler who tends subjects; this proverb tells the keeper to know the condition of his flocks and attend to his herds, turning oversight into concrete attention.

basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
note: The instruction requires sustained, informed attention to a herd, closely matching the source's B003 extension from shepherding to watching where a matter is going.

basis: riches and crown do not endure
note: Following the flock-watch instruction, the proverb states that wealth and political standing are not permanent; its own transience claim clarifies why the source calls pasture provision temporary metāʿ.

basis: old grass passes and new growth appears
note: The pastoral maxim traces hay's disappearance, fresh growth, and mountain vegetation; it offers a close agrarian counterpart to pasture brought forth and then transformed.

basis: Owned people and pasture sheep
note: The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and presents a protected pasture; the psalm says Israel is God’s people and sheep of his pasture, explicitly uniting ownership and flock.

basis: we are his; people and sheep of his pasture
note: The verse joins belonging to the creator with being the sheep of his pasture, directly combining the source's Rab-as-owner with its herd and grazing scene.

basis: Human life like grass
note: The commentary reads the pasture’s decay toward the temporary world; human days are compared to grass here, and flourishing to a field flower, carrying the vegetation image into mortality.

basis: The place no longer knows it
note: The commentary makes the pasture’s transformation a sign of transience; after wind passes over the field-flower, its place knows it no more, sharpening the image of disappearance.

basis: Grass for cattle
note: The commentary says the Lord brings forth pasture and that its root-family includes grazing animals; YHWH causes grass to grow for cattle, closely matching divine provision of fodder.

basis: grass for cattle; plants and food for humans
note: The psalm treats the sprouting of grass for cattle and human food as God's work, closely matching the source's creator of pasture and its 79:33 and 80:31 provision motif.

basis: Creatures await provision
note: The commentary’s owner produces pasture for dependent herds; all creatures here look to God for food in its season, adding ongoing dependence to the created pasture scene.

basis: God grows grass
note: The commentary links God’s act of bringing forth pasture with a shepherd’s provision; YHWH covers the sky with clouds and makes grass grow on the mountains, naming the growth as God’s work.

basis: rain makes grass grow on mountains
note: God covers the sky, prepares rain, and sprouts grass on the mountains; this connects divine production of grazing land with the commentary's mountain-and-pasture association.

basis: Food for animals
note: The commentary connects pasture with guarded livestock; God gives animals their food, even young ravens when they cry, extending the provision beyond a human flock.

basis: God gives food to beasts
note: The creator's provision of food to animals makes explicit the care for livestock that the source reads into pasture.

basis: Personal shepherd and owner
note: The commentary says Rab is owner and later notes one who names “his Lord”; David calls YHWH “my shepherd,” making ownership a personal relation of trust.

basis: Rab as flock-owner and shepherd
note: The psalm names YHWH as the speaker's shepherd, giving the source's Rab who owns and directs the herd a direct divine pastoral frame.

basis: Green pasture and leading
note: The commentary joins the one who guides a flock to protected pasture; YHWH makes the speaker lie down in green pastures and leads him beside waters, furnishing the same pastoral sequence.

basis: green pastures and resting waters
note: The shepherd brings the dependent flock to nourishing pasture and rest, closely matching the commentary's owner who brings the herd to a protected grazing place.

basis: Guidance and correction
note: The commentary’s Rab can mean one who sets things right and its guidance image leads the herd; here the shepherd restores the soul and leads in right paths, linking care with moral direction.

basis: restore and guide in right paths
note: The same shepherd restores and leads the person on paths; this makes the source's هدى B003 front-leading image part of pastoral care rather than mere travel.

basis: Protection in danger
note: The commentary glosses the shepherd as surrounding and protecting livestock; the speaker fears no evil in the dark valley because YHWH is with him and uses rod and staff to comfort him.

basis: shepherd and carry God's inheritance forever
note: The plea asks God to save, bless, shepherd, and carry his people forever; it makes protective pastoral rule explicitly enduring, relevant to the source's turn from temporary pasture to what lasts.

basis: Owner of livestock
note: The commentary calls Rab the owner of everything and evokes a herd; God says every forest animal and cattle on a thousand hills are his, giving the ownership claim concrete scope.

basis: cattle on a thousand hills are mine
note: God's claim over cattle supplies a concrete biblical form for the commentary's insistence that Rab is the owner before he is the herd's guide.

basis: Wild herd under divine knowledge
note: The commentary includes a wild-cattle herd under the r-b-b word family; God says he knows every bird of the mountains and the creatures of the field are his, extending divine ownership to wild creatures.

basis: Creation belongs to God
note: The commentary’s Rab means owner of everything; God says the world and all it contains are his, grounding the pasture scene in universal possession.

basis: Pastures clothed with flocks
note: The commentary presents a pasture brought forth for a herd; the psalm depicts pastures clothed with flocks and valleys covered with grain, adding an image of abundance to divine provision.

basis: pastures clothed with flocks and fields sing
note: Pastures are filled with flocks and the fertile landscape shouts and sings; it lets the source's opening praise encompass the very pasture and herd that God causes to thrive.

basis: Moses and Aaron lead God's people like a flock
note: The psalm says God led the people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, giving the commentary's Moses-linked scene a divine owner, human agents, and flock in one verse.

basis: Moses leads Israel like a flock
note: The commentary points to Moses’ pastoral reply to Pharaoh and develops guidance of a herd; the psalm recalls God leading his people like a flock by Moses and Aaron, placing the image in the Exodus story.

basis: God leads his flock
note: The commentary makes the owner, the ones leading ahead, and pasture parts of one scene; God brings Israel out like sheep and leads them through the wilderness, joining divine guidance to flock imagery.

basis: God leads people as sheep and guides them as flock
note: The wilderness exodus is described with both flock-leading and guidance, closely matching the source's single work of owner, guide, and herd.

basis: Safe guidance
note: The commentary says the shepherd protects the animals he guides; Israel is led safely here, with the sea overwhelming its enemies, pairing guidance with protection.

basis: David brought from tending sheep
note: The commentary links the shepherd of animals to the ruler of people; God takes David from following nursing ewes to shepherd Jacob, making the transition from literal flock care to leadership explicit.

basis: David shepherds and guides Israel
note: The commentary’s flock leaders guide those behind them and its ruler tends subjects; David shepherds Israel with an upright heart and guides them with skillful hands, uniting care and guidance.

basis: David shepherds with integrity and skillful guidance
note: David's shepherding is defined by inner integrity and skilled leading, developing the source's claim that pastoral language can describe competent public rule.

basis: flock of God's pasture gives thanks forever
note: The flock-of-your-pasture formula culminates in perpetual thanksgiving; it brings the source's opening glorification of the Rab into the pastoral relation itself.

basis: Shepherd leading Joseph
note: The commentary’s owner-guiding-a-flock scene is directly named in the address to the Shepherd of Israel, who leads Joseph like a flock; the prayer turns the image into a plea for divine attention.

basis: Shepherd of Israel leads Joseph like a flock
note: The invocation directly addresses God as Israel's shepherd and asks him to lead Joseph as a flock, concentrating the source's owner and front-leading functions.

basis: Grass as a brief life-image
note: The commentary moves from pasture becoming debris to the temporary life of this world; this psalm compares people to grass swept away, connecting vegetation’s short life to human transience.

basis: Grass withers by evening
note: The commentary says pasture is turned into waste; the psalm’s grass sprouts in the morning and withers by evening, giving a daily image of swift change.

basis: evil-doers sprout like grass only for destruction
note: The psalm uses flourishing grass for a short-lived prosperity that ends in destruction, closely paralleling the source's pasture that becomes debris and its warning about transient life.

basis: the Most High is forever
note: The contrast calls YHWH the Most High forever, joining the source's al-Aʿlā title to its contrast between fading grass and enduring reality.

basis: People as pasture flock
note: The commentary joins ownership, care, and pasture; the psalm calls worshippers the people of God’s pasture and sheep of his hand, adding belonging to the grazing image.

basis: people of God's pasture and sheep of his hand
note: The verse makes Israel both God's people and the sheep held in his hand; its call to hear his voice joins ownership, pastoral care, and responsive recognition of the Rab.

basis: foolish shepherd neither seeks, heals, nor nourishes
note: The false shepherd neglects the lost and injured and consumes the fat flock instead; this negative portrait tests every protective and provisioning element developed in the source.
